content: Resistance to antiretroviral therapy (ART) in individuals living with HIV significantly undermines the effectiveness of treatment, often resulting in virological failure and increased mortality. Antiretroviral drug resistance testing, which can be either genotypic or phenotypic, is utilized to guide the selection of ART regimens. These tests are typically performed either at the initiation of therapy or when treatment failure occurs. While resistance testing is widely implemented in high-income countries, its use is limited in resource-constrained settings. The primary objective of this systematic review was to assess the effectiveness of antiretroviral resistance testing in reducing mortality and morbidity among HIV-positive individuals. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies that compared resistance testing to no resistance testing, regardless of prior ART exposure. The primary outcomes of interest were mortality and virological failure, while secondary outcomes included changes in CD4-T-lymphocyte count, progression to AIDS, development of new opportunistic infections, changes in viral load, and quality of life. The review identified 11 RCTs, published between 1999 and 2006, involving a total of 2531 participants. All participants had prior exposure to ART, and no observational studies were found. The trials varied in follow-up duration (ranging from 12 to 150 weeks), study settings, and types of resistance testing. Seven studies employed genotypic testing, two used phenotypic testing, and two utilized both methods. All studies were conducted in Europe, the USA, or South America, and only one study received funding from a manufacturer of resistance tests. The findings indicated that resistance testing had little or no impact on mortality (odds ratio [OR] 0.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36 to 2.22; moderate-certainty evidence). It may have slightly reduced the likelihood of virological failure (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.87; low-certainty evidence). Resistance testing likely had minimal or no effect on changes in CD4 cell count (mean difference [MD] -1.00 cells/mm³, 95% CI -12.49 to 10.50; moderate-certainty evidence) or progression to AIDS (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.29; moderate-certainty evidence). Additionally, resistance testing had little or no effect on adverse events (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.55; low-certainty evidence) but probably reduced viral load (MD -0.23, 95% CI -0.35 to -0.11; moderate-certainty evidence). None of the studies reported on the development of new opportunistic infections or quality of life. The review found no significant heterogeneity in outcomes, with I² values ranging from 0% to 25%. Subgroup analyses revealed no differences based on the type of resistance testing (genotypic versus phenotypic), the inclusion of expert advice in interpreting resistance tests, or participant age. Mortality outcomes were consistent across studies with varying risks of bias. In conclusion, resistance testing likely improved virological outcomes in individuals with virological failure in trials conducted over 12 years ago. However, there was no evidence to support its use in treatment-naive individuals. Resistance testing did not demonstrate significant benefits in reducing mortality or progression to AIDS. Furthermore, the trials included very few participants from lowand middle-income countries, limiting the generalizability of the findings to these settings.
